chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: Dionysus. I have arrived here in Thebes: Dionysus, the son of Zeus, whom Semelê, Kadmus' daughter, bore when lightning drove her into labour. I have exchanged my divine appearance for a human one and stand beside the springs of Dirkê and the waters of Ismenus. Near the palace I can see my mother's grave, where the thunderbolt struck her. The wreckage of her house still smoulders with Zeus's fire, the enduring mark of Hera's violence against my mother. Kadmus has rightly made this ground, his daughter's burial place, a sanctuary. I myself have enclosed it in the thick green growth of vines. I left the gold-rich fields of Lydia and Phrygia and travelled across the sun-scorched Persian country, past Bactrian fortresses and the storm-beaten land of Media, onwards through blessed Araby and all Asia beside the salt sea, with its crowds of lofty-towered cities where Hellenes live among foreign peoples. Of the cities of Hellas, this is the first I visit. In those other countries I established my dances and ceremonies to reveal myself to people as a God. Here in Hellas, Thebes was the first place I stirred with my triumphant cry, dressing her in fawnskin and putting the ivy-covered thyrsus into her hand. For my mother's sisters—shame upon them!—declared that Zeus had never fathered Dionysus. Semelê, they said, had slept with a mortal and blamed Zeus for her own lust, a clever deception devised by Kadmus! That was why, they boasted, Zeus killed the lying woman who claimed him as her lover. So I have driven them from home with the sting of madness. They live distracted in the mountains, compelled to wear the clothing of my celebrations. Every woman of Kadmus' people, every one, I drove raving out of her house. They sit among Kadmus' sons beneath green pine trees on exposed rocks. Thebes must learn, however unwillingly, what it means to remain outside my sacred mysteries. I must defend Semelê's honour, revealing to mortals the God she bore to Zeus. Now Kadmus has handed his crown and royal authority to Pentheus, another daughter's son. In attacking me he fights heaven itself: he excludes me from his offerings of wine and leaves my name out of his prayers. I will therefore demonstrate my divinity to him and to all Thebes. Once I have triumphed here, I will move to another country and reveal myself there. If the angry Thebans take up weapons to drive their Bacchants from the mountains, I will lead my Maenads against them in battle. That is why I have assumed a mortal body and changed my appearance to a man's. Women who left Tmolus, Lydia's wall of rock, my company of revellers whom I brought from foreign homes to share my travels and my rest, raise the cymbals invented by great Mother Rhea and myself, the instruments of Phrygian towns. Surround Pentheus' royal palace and strike them so that Kadmus' city may witness it. I will go into Kithairon's valleys, where my Bacchanals are living, and dance with them there. (He leaves. The Chorus enters, waving thyrsus-wands and striking their timbrels.)

chapters.title: Parodos
paragraphs: Chorus. From the soil of Asia, far across Tmolus' sacred ridges, I hasten to the work I love, the labour that brings me no pain, serving the King of Clamour and singing my welcome to the Bacchanals' God.

Chorus. Who is blocking the road? Who is still inside the house? Come out! Let everyone make their lips holy by closing them to irreverent speech. Now I will sing his praises, sounding the hymn that Dionysus himself commands.

Chorus. Happy the person granted the blessing of instruction in heaven's mysteries, whose life is pure and whose soul is swept by the ever-wakeful sacred dance! Holy cleansing fits him to join the Bacchanals racing over the mountains and the secret ceremonies of Cybelê, the ancient Mother. Crowned with sprays of ivy, he lifts his thyrsus high and sings to honour the God of the Vine. Come, you Bacchanals, come! Bring the King of Clamour, a God's child who walked the Phrygian mountains, home to the broad roads of Hellas, bring him home!

Chorus. His mother bore this God as she died. The irresistible pain of childbirth tore her, carrying her towards death on the wings of Zeus's descending thunder. He was born before his time as her life went out, struck by the falling flame. But Zeus Kronion received his child into another chamber of birth. Hidden in a fold of his thigh, fastened shut with golden clasps, the baby lay concealed from Hera's gaze until the day appointed by the Fates. Then Zeus brought forth a God with the horns of a bull and wound snakes through his hair. That is why his Maenads, too, wear serpents among their locks.

Chorus. Thebes, the town that nursed Semelê, put an ivy crown upon your forehead. Blossom inside the rich green bryony with its star-shaped flowers, and weave oak and pine among your hair in the rapture of Bacchus. Trim your spotted fawnskin with shining white wool, hanging in silvery tassels. Servants of Bacchus, swing your wild wands high! The whole country will become a single company of dancers when the King of Clamour leads his revellers into the mountains, the mountains where your women wait for him, driven from their shuttles and looms by the Vine-god who pursued them in their frenzied flight.

Chorus. O cave that echoed with the Curetes' songs, chamber where the infant Zeus was born! There the Corybants, their helmet-crests flashing as they danced through the dark underground halls, discovered this timbrel with its circle of stretched hide that our hands beat. They joined its Bacchic joy to the sweet, high call of Phrygian flutes and placed its thunder in Rhea's hands, lifting it above the roar of celebration. But the gift passed from the Mother to the raving band of Satyrs. Those wild woodland creatures gave Semelê's child the worship he delights in, joining the clash of timbrels to the flash of white dancing feet at every third year's festival.

Chorus. What a transport of delight when someone swerves away from the Bacchanals racing through the mountains and sinks down on the ground, covered by the holy garment of a spotted fawnskin! Wearing it, he has hunted the goat to death for its blood, for a taste of the steaming raw feast, while wild feet hurry across the hills of Lydia and Phrygia. The King of Clamour leads us, thrilling our hearts with his cry of "Evoë!" The earth streams with milk, with wine, with the nectar of bees, and smoke rises like the incense of Araby. The Bacchanal raises his flaming pine torch and sweeps it through the air, shouting to the scattered revellers as fire pours from its tip. On he runs, on he dances, shaking his curls loose to the wind, and his voice cuts clearly through the roaring company: "Forward, you Bacchanals! Forward, Bacchanal girls, glory of Tmolus with its springs of gold. Join your singing voices to the thunder of the timbrels. Ring out the happy God's happy praises in Phrygian cries and song, while that fountain of melody rises, the sacred flutes pouring their music far and wide, their notes keeping time with the feet that climb the pilgrim road into the mountains!" Enraptured, the Bacchanal woman races onwards, her feet skipping swiftly like foals gambolling about mares that graze in the meadows. (Teiresias enters.)

chapters.title: First Episode
paragraphs: Teiresias. Ho, gatekeeper! Call Kadmus out of the house, Agenor's son who came from Sidon and surrounded this Theban city with towers. Someone go and tell him Teiresias wants him. He knows why I am here: the agreement one old man made with another still older, to wind ivy round our thyrsi, put on fawnskins and crown our heads with ivy wreaths. (Kadmus enters.)

Kadmus. Dear friend, I heard your voice inside the house and recognised it: wisdom speaking with a wise man's voice. Here I am, ready and dressed in the God's clothing. Dionysus is my own daughter's son, and he has revealed his divinity to mankind. We must do everything in our power to honour him. Where shall we dance, where set our feet and shake our grey heads? Teach me, Teiresias; let one old man guide another, for you are wise. Night and day I can strike the ground with my thyrsus without growing tired. Joy makes us forget how old we are.
Teiresias. My heart feels exactly as yours does. I too feel young; I will try the dance.
Kadmus. Then let us ride in a chariot to the mountain.
Teiresias. No, that would lessen the honour we give the God!
Kadmus. One old man leading another, I will take you along.
Teiresias. We will feel no weariness; the God will guide us there.
Kadmus. Will we be the only Thebans dancing for Bacchus?
Teiresias. Yes; wisdom belongs to us alone. All the others are fools.
Kadmus. We have delayed long enough. Come, take hold of my hand.
Teiresias. Here it is; link your hand firmly with mine.
Kadmus. Mortal as I am, I will never look down on the Gods!

Teiresias. The Gods are beyond our reasoning. We hold to the traditions of our fathers, ancient as time, and no argument will overthrow them, however subtle the minds that produce it. Someone may say I show no respect for my age by putting on ivy and preparing to dance. But the God has made no distinction between the dancing of the young and of those bent by years. From everyone equally he demands the honour owed to him. He has no wish to receive only half his due.

Kadmus. Since your eyes cannot see the daylight, Teiresias, I will speak for you as circumstances require. Here comes Pentheus, Echion's son, hurrying towards the palace; I gave him the throne. How agitated he is! What strange news can he have? (Pentheus enters.)

Pentheus. While I was away from this country I heard of extraordinary misconduct in my own city. Our women have left their homes, pretending to be possessed by Bacchus, and wander wildly over the wooded hills, dancing in honour of this new God Dionysus, whoever he is. In the middle of each company stand bowls filled to the brim with wine. They slip away, some here and some there, to secluded places where they commit shameful acts with men. They claim to be Maenad priestesses, but it is Aphroditê they honour more than Bacchus. My servants are keeping all those I have caught securely chained in the public prison. I will hunt the rest down from the hills: Ino, Agavê who bore me to Echion, and Autonoê, Aktaion's mother. Once iron bonds have caught them, this poisonous Bacchic revelry will soon stop. I hear that a stranger has arrived from Lydia, a conjurer and sorcerer with perfumed golden curls tossed about his head, flushed with wine, his eyes carrying Love's seductive charm. Day and night he keeps company with the girls, pretending to perform Evian mysteries. If I can imprison him inside these walls, that will end his thyrsus-beating and his flowing locks: I will cut his head from his shoulders. He calls Dionysus a God! He says Zeus once sewed him into his thigh, although lightning destroyed him and his mother because she lied about Zeus loving her. Doesn't blasphemy like that deserve the terrible punishment of hanging, whoever this stranger may be? But here is another marvel: Teiresias the prophet, dressed in spotted fawnskins! And my mother's father too—what a laughable spectacle! Shaking a reed-wand! Grandfather, I am ashamed to see grey heads emptied of all sense. Throw away that ivy, drop the thyrsus and free your hand, my mother's father. Teiresias, you persuaded him to do this. You want to force this new God on people so that you can earn money from augury and prophecy! If your white hair did not protect you, you would sit chained among the Bacchanals for introducing these pestilent ceremonies. When the glory of the grape joins a women's feast, I say nothing good comes from their celebrations.
Chorus. What blasphemy! Stranger, have you no respect for heaven or for Kadmus, who sowed the earth-born seed? Echion's son, you disgrace your ancestry!

Teiresias. A wise man readily finds eloquence when his subject is noble. Your tongue runs smoothly enough to sound wise, but nothing you have said makes sense. A reckless man with power and a ready tongue is a bad citizen because he lacks judgement. As for this new God you ridicule, words cannot express the greatness he will attain in Hellas. Prince, two powers stand foremost among humanity. There is divine Demeter: she is Earth, whichever name you choose to give her, and she feeds mortals with solid food. Then comes Semelê's son. To complement her gift he discovered the flowing drink of the grape and gave it to human beings. When that stream of wine fills sorrow-worn people, it rests them from their grief. He gives them sleep too, forgetfulness of everyday suffering; there is no other salve for their toil. Though himself a God, he is poured out as an offering to the Gods, and through him people receive blessings. You mock the tale of his being sewn into Zeus's thigh? Let me show you the beauty of that story. After Zeus rescued the baby from the lightning fire and carried him to Olympus, Hera wanted to cast the divine child out of heaven. Zeus devised a God's countermeasure. He broke off a piece of the air surrounding the earth and shaped it into a hostage, keeping Dionysus safe from Hera's malice. Later people said he had been nursed in Zeus's thigh. They changed the name and made a myth from it, because the God had once served as a hostage to Hera. This God also foretells the future: Bacchic frenzy and ecstasy overflow with prophecy. When his full power floods our bodies, he makes his maddened followers tell what is to come. He shares some of Ares' powers as well. Armoured armies drawn up for battle are struck with panic before they touch a spear. That too is madness sent by Dionysus. You will yet see him on Delphi's cliffs, leaping across the cleft summit with pine torches and waving Bacchus' branch high above him. Yes, he will be great throughout Hellas. Listen to me, Pentheus. Do not boast that sheer force commands humanity, or imagine yourself wise because your distorted vision tells you so. Welcome the God into your country. Pour wine, join his dances and put on a wreath. Dionysus will not impose chastity on women. Restraint in every matter always rests in the nature of true womanhood. Remember this: a woman with a virtuous heart will not be corrupted by his rites. You enjoy it when thousands gather at your gates and all Thebes glorifies the name of Pentheus. He too, I believe, enjoys being honoured. Kadmus and I, the pair you mock, will crown ourselves with ivy and dance. We are two old men, but dance we must. Nothing you say will persuade me to fight the Gods. Your madness is severe; no spell can cure you, even if spells have driven you mad.
Chorus. Old man, your words do honour to Phœbus, and your wisdom pays proper reverence to the mighty God Bromius.

Kadmus. My son, Teiresias has given you good advice. Stay within our customary way of life, beside us. Your mind is wandering in the clouds; your wisdom amounts to nothing. Even if, as you claim, he is no God, call him one. Let a splendid deception give Semelê the reputation of having borne a God, and our whole house will share the honour. Do you remember Aktaion's miserable end? The dogs he had raised tore him apart in the meadows and devoured his raw flesh because he boasted that he hunted better than Artemis. To save you from the same fate, let me crown your head with ivy. Join us in honouring the God.

Pentheus. Take your hand away! Go and play the Bacchanal without smearing me with your foolishness. I will punish this prophet who has taught you to be senseless. Someone go quickly. (To an attendant.) You, hurry to his place of divination. Use levers to wrench it up and throw it down. Turn the whole thing upside down; scatter his holy ribbons to the winds and storms. That will wound him most deeply. Others of you search the city for that stranger with the girl's face, who infects our wives with strange madness and dishonours our beds. If you find him, drag him here in chains. He will be stoned to death and regret ever celebrating his rites in Thebes.

Teiresias. Poor wretch, you have no idea what you have said! You lacked sense before; now you are utterly mad. Kadmus, let us go and pray for him, savage brute though he is, and for Thebes, so that no extraordinary vengeance from the God strikes them. Come with me, carrying your ivy staff. Try to support my body as I support yours. What a disgrace if two greybeards fell! Still, what does that matter? We must serve Bacchus, Zeus's son. Kadmus, take care that Pentheus does not bring his name's echo, repentance, upon your house. It is his own behaviour speaking here, no prophecy. Only a fool speaks foolishly. (They leave.)

chapters.title: First Stasimon
paragraphs: Chorus. O Holiness, ruling even over the Gods, yet bending your golden wing down towards us on the earth, do you hear the king's words? Do you hear Pentheus blasting his defiance against the King of Clamour, his blasphemous abuse of Semelê's son, foremost of the blessed Gods at the beautiful feast? It is his special privilege to call our feet into the dance, where light laughter mingles with flutes and the children of sorrow forget their tears. Whenever the glory of the grape appears at the banquet people offer to the high Gods, the wine bowl spreads the cloak of sleep over ivy-crowned revellers drinking deeply.

Chorus. Unbridled mouths that acknowledge no restraint and stubborn folly that strays beyond the bounds of law share a single end: disaster. But a life as peaceful as a summer day, and footsteps guided by good judgement, stand firm and steady; they remain the support of the household. Though the heavenly beings live far away, they look down on humanity from their cloudy doorways. Knowledge cannot purchase wisdom. The spirit that rises beyond a mortal's proper height has few days to live. Anyone who grasps at things beyond human reach will lose even the blessings already secured. Such paths, it seems to me, belong to wandering, witless madness.

Chorus. If only I could escape to Aphroditê's home in Cyprus, that island paradise surrounded by the sea, where the Love-gods weave their powerful enchantments over the soul; or to the fields of uncountable golden harvests, watered by the seven-mouthed river, where rain has never fallen! Better still, to the land of incomparable beauty, Pieria, where the Muses make their home and sing! Lead me there, King of Clamour, to stand without fear on holy Olympus! God of Revels, guide me to the dwelling of the Graces and Desire, where nobody forbids the Bacchanals to dance in their circle.

Chorus. Our God, Zeus's offspring, delights in the happy feast where his cups gleam. He loves Peace, the giver of riches, the divine mother who nurses Youth. His generous gift of wine brings joy that ends sorrow to the lowly and the great alike. But he hates the person who scorns a life whose days and nights fly on the wings of happiness and refuses to choose its blessings. Wisdom tells us to keep our distance from excessive cleverness. For me the people's heartfelt faith, alive in their daily dealings in the marketplace, is enough. (Pentheus returns. A Servant and attendants enter with Dionysus in bonds.)

chapters.title: Second Episode
paragraphs: Servant. Pentheus, we have returned with the prey you sent us to pursue; our mission succeeded. The wild creature proved tame. He made no dash for freedom, but willingly held out his hands. He did not turn pale; the rosy colour stayed in his cheeks. Smiling, he told us to tie him up and take him away, and waited there to make my job easy. Ashamed, I told him, "Stranger, I am taking you against my own wishes, under Pentheus' orders." The Bacchanals you captured and chained in the public prison have escaped their bonds and run into the meadows. There they dance and call upon the God Bromius. Their fetters fell apart by themselves; the doors unbarred themselves without a human hand. This man has certainly brought many wonders to Thebes! What happens next is for you to decide.

Pentheus. Untie his hands. Now he is caught in the net, he will not be quick enough to get away from me. Ha! You are certainly handsome enough to tempt women, stranger, which is why you have come to Thebes. Those flowing locks falling so seductively down your cheeks show you are no wrestler. Your carefully tended skin is white, untouched by sunlight, kept pale in the shade while you hunt for desire using beauty as your bait. First tell me which country you come from.
Dionysus. There is no need to boast; the answer is simple. Perhaps you know flower-covered Tmolus.
Pentheus. Yes; it surrounds the city where the Sardians live.
Dionysus. That is where I come from. My native country is Lydia.
Pentheus. Why have you brought these ceremonies into Hellas?
Dionysus. Zeus's son Dionysus initiated me into them.
Pentheus. Is there a Zeus over there fathering a new set of gods?
Dionysus. No, the very Zeus who married Semelê in this place.
Pentheus. Did you become his servant awake or in a dream?
Dionysus. We were face to face when he gave me his mysteries.
Pentheus. Well, what exactly are these mysteries like?
Dionysus. Only people who have been initiated may know.
Pentheus. What benefit do his worshippers gain from them?
Dionysus. You are forbidden to hear, though knowing would be worthwhile.
Pentheus. A clever sham to make me eager to hear more!
Dionysus. His ceremonies reject anyone who acts without reverence.
Pentheus. You saw the God: what did his appearance look like?
Dionysus. Whatever he chose it to be. That was no decision of mine.
Pentheus. Another clever dodge; you have told me nothing again.
Dionysus. To foolish ears, a sensible answer sounds like nonsense.
Pentheus. Were you the first to bring his divine presence here?
Dionysus. The people of all Asia take part in these mystic dances.
Pentheus. Yes, and they have far less wisdom than the Hellenes.
Dionysus. In this they have much more. Their customs differ from yours.
Pentheus. Do you celebrate his ceremonies at night or during daylight?
Dionysus. Usually after dark; darkness deepens their solemnity.
Pentheus. And it sets traps of lust for women as well.
Dionysus. Schemes of lust can be planned in daylight too.
Pentheus. Your disgusting evasions will now earn their punishment.
Dionysus. As will your foolishness and your lack of reverence.
Pentheus. What a bold Bacchant, so skilful at fencing with words!
Dionysus. What sentence awaits me? How do you intend to take revenge?
Pentheus. I shall begin by shearing off those pretty curls of yours.
Dionysus. My hair is sacred; I have grown it for the God.
Pentheus. Next you will surrender the thyrsus you are holding in your hands.
Dionysus. Take it yourself; that staff belongs to Dionysus.
Pentheus. I shall keep your body locked inside my prison.
Dionysus. Whenever I choose, the God himself will set me free.
Pentheus. Yes, when you call on him among your Bacchanals!
Dionysus. Indeed, he is close by now, observing this insult.
Pentheus. Where, then? He certainly isn't visible to my eyes.
Dionysus. Here beside me. Your impiety keeps you from seeing him.
Pentheus. Arrest him! The man is making a mockery of me and Thebes.
Dionysus. Don't tie me up! That is reason giving folly a warning.
Pentheus. My order is to bind him; my authority outweighs yours.
Dionysus. You understand neither the life you lead nor who you truly are.
Pentheus. I am Pentheus, son of Agavê and Echion.
Dionysus. A fitting name for someone who will be pent up in misery.

Pentheus. Take him away! Lock him in the nearby horses' stalls, where he will see nothing but darkness. He can dance there! These women you brought as accomplices to your crimes I shall sell into slavery or put to work as my weavers. That will silence their hands, their clashing cymbals and their beating drums.

Dionysus. I am going. No fate that Fate has forbidden can ever reach me. Dionysus, whose existence you denied, will punish you for these insults. When you abuse me, it is he whom you drag into bondage. (Dionysus leaves under guard; Pentheus also leaves.)

chapters.title: Second Stasimon
paragraphs: Chorus. Greetings, maiden Dirkê, majestic, blessed daughter of Acheloüs! Long ago your cool, silvery waters received the child of Zeus, when his father snatched him from the unquenchable lightning and sealed the baby inside his thigh. The Father called aloud, "Come, Dithyrambus! Enter this womb that belongs to no mother. By this name I now proclaim you to Thebes, God of the Bacchanals." Yet, Dirkê, you drive me away when I bring you the glorious sight of his garlanded celebrations! Why am I rejected, disowned and hated? I swear by the abundant clustered beauty of Dionysus' vine that the time will come when your heart welcomes Dionysus and acknowledges him as its lord.

Chorus. Look how Pentheus reveals his earth-born ancestry, betraying the taint of that ancient dragon's blood, the serpent descended from the earth-born Titan Echion. It has made him a grim-faced monster, like the savage race of giants who fought the immortals, rather than a child of mortal parents. He intends to tie me up at once, though I am Bromius' servant. Today he has imprisoned my companion in the revels inside his palace, shut up in darkness! Dionysus, Zeus's son, can you not see his actions, your prophets struggling against tyranny? Rush down the side of Olympus, brandishing your golden thyrsus. Come to us, our King, and restrain this murderous man's insolent rage.

Chorus. Where are you lingering? On Nysa, mother of wild animals, waving your wand to urge your revellers forward? On the peaks of Corycia reaching towards heaven? Or in the remote forests enfolding Olympus' slopes, where Orpheus once played his harp with such mastery that trees and wild beasts gathered around him in adoration? Three times blessed is the land of Pieria; Evius does you honour! See, he is coming, coming at the head of his dances with Bacchanal songs. Swiftly he will cross the waters of Axius, marshalling his Maenads' leaping feet into the sweeping circles of the dance. He will hasten across Lydias, father of rivers and giver of blessings, whose lovely waters, the story says, roll through the country of brave warhorses and make the land fertile all around.
Dionysus (within). Ho there! Listen to my voice, listen! My Bacchanal company, my Bacchanal company! (The members of the Chorus answer one at a time.)
Chorus 1. What was that cry? Where did it sound from? That was my Evian King's voice!
Dionysus (within). Ho there! Ho there! Once again I call to you, Semelê's child, the offspring of Zeus.

Chorus 2. Ho there! Our master, our master! Ho there! Come now to your celebrating company, King of Clamour, King of Clamour! (An earthquake.) Earth beneath us, are you rocking back and forth? What a tremendous convulsion! Pentheus' palace will soon be shaken to pieces and come crashing down!
Chorus 3. Inside that palace Dionysus is revealing himself as a God! Give him your reverent worship.
Chorus 4. We bow down before him. (An earthquake.) Look at the stone lintels swaying above those pillars! Now the King of Clamour will send his victorious cry ringing through the palace.
Dionysus (within). Light the glaring red torch of the thunderbolt. Let flames spread all around the palace of Pentheus. (A great blaze of light surrounds the palace and Semelê's monument.)

Chorus 5. Ah! Can you not see the raging fire wrapped around the sacred tomb? Look closely: Semelê, struck by thunder, left it as the memorial of her destruction by Zeus's lightning. Throw yourselves to the ground, Maenads, throw down your bodies trembling with terrible fear! Our King is coming, the child of Zeus, to throw that palace into turmoil and ruin. (The Chorus falls face down. Dionysus comes out of the palace.)

chapters.title: Third Episode
paragraphs: Dionysus. Women of Asia, has pure terror overwhelmed you so completely that you have collapsed on the ground? I suppose you saw Pentheus' palace sway when Bacchus shook it. Come, get up from the earth and shake this bewildering fear out of your bodies.
Chorus. Welcome, brightest light of our Evian celebrations! I was so lonely and abandoned; what joy it is to see you now!
Dionysus. Did fear make your hearts fail when I went inside? Did you think I would sink into darkness, trapped in Pentheus' prison?
Chorus. Why wouldn't we? What protection would I have if disaster overtook you? But how did you escape from that godless tyrant's power?
Dionysus. I set myself free, quite easily, without any labour or struggle.
Chorus. But didn't he fasten your hands in layer upon layer of chains?

Dionysus. I made him ridiculous. He imagined he was binding me, but never touched or held me; he was feeding on an empty illusion. Beside the stalls where he meant to lock me up he found a bull and began looping his ropes round its knees and hoofs. He panted with rage, sweat pouring from his whole body, biting his lips, while I sat calmly beside him and watched at my leisure. Just then our Bacchus arrived. He shook the house as if with an earthquake and kindled a sudden fire upon his mother's grave. The king thought his palace was burning. He rushed everywhere, frantically ordering his servants to fetch water. Every slave was busy with that useless task. Then he abandoned it, thinking I had escaped his trap, and rushed into the building with his deadly sword drawn. Bromius, I believe—I can only tell you what I think—created a phantom inside the house. Pentheus immediately threw himself upon it, charging and stabbing the luminous air, convinced he was killing me. Then Bacchus dealt his pride another humiliation by throwing the building to the ground. It lies there now in ruins, a sight to make him bitterly regret my chains! Exhausted by his efforts, he drops his sword and collapses. A mortal dared to challenge a God in battle! I then walked out unhindered, without troubling myself about Pentheus, and have come from his palace to you. But I think he will be out here soon: I can hear footsteps inside. What will he say about this? However fiercely he rages, I shall take his blustering lightly. Wisdom means keeping anger under sober control. (Pentheus enters.)

Pentheus. What an outrage! The stranger has escaped, although a moment ago his chains held him as firmly as fate. Ha! There he is! What is going on? How did you get out to stand in front of my own palace?
Dionysus. Stay where you are, and slow the pace of your anger.
Pentheus. How did you get out here after escaping from your chains?
Dionysus. Didn't you hear me say, "Someone will set me free"?
Pentheus. Who? Your answers grow stranger every time you speak.
Dionysus. The one who makes the grape-bearing vine grow for humankind.
Pentheus. Yes, who sends women raving out of their houses!
Dionysus. What you ridicule is the very glory of Dionysus.
Pentheus (to attendants). My order is to bar every tower around us.
Dionysus. What for? Can the Gods not cross over walls?
Pentheus. Clever, so clever—except in the things where you need wisdom.

Dionysus. I have wisdom where it matters most. But first listen to that man and hear his account. He has come with news from the mountains. I will wait for you; don't worry that I might run away. (A Herdman enters.)
Herdman. Pentheus, ruler of this country of Thebes, I have come from Kithairon, where the glittering silver arrows of the snow never fail.
Pentheus. What important news have you come here to bring?

Herdman. I have seen the frenzied Bacchanals whose white feet carried them away from this country. King, I want to tell you and Thebes what extraordinary and astonishing things they are doing. But first tell me whether I may speak freely about what I saw or must shorten the sail of my story. I fear your hasty temper, your passion and your anger that exceeds even a king's measure.

Pentheus. Speak; you will leave unharmed by me. Honest men must not be met with anger. The more dreadful your account of the Bacchanals, the more severely I will punish the man who taught our women this wickedness.

Herdman. Your grazing cattle were climbing the steep hillside just as the sun first sent out its warming rays, when I saw three companies of Bacchant women. Autonoë led one, your mother Agavê another, and Ino the third. They all lay sleeping, their bodies resting easily. Some leaned back on leafy pine branches; others lay carelessly on the ground with oak leaves under their heads. They were modest, not drunk on wine, as you claim, nor chasing desire alone through the woodland shade to the sighing of flutes. When the lowing of our horned cattle reached her, your mother leapt up among the Bacchanals and shouted, "Shake off your sleep!" Brushing rosy sleep from their eyelids, they sprang up, wonderfully graceful to see: young girls, elderly women and unmarried maidens. First they let their hair fall over their shoulders. Those whose fawnskins had come unfastened tied them up, girdling the spotted hides with snakes that licked their cheeks. Some held fawns or wolf cubs in their arms and fed these wild creatures with their own white breast milk. They were young mothers who had left their babies, their breasts still full. Then they crowned their heads with ivy, oak leaves and star-flowered bryony. One woman struck the rock with her thyrsus and a fountain burst out in a shower of spray. Another drove her reed-wand into the earth and the God sent a spring of wine up through it. Those who wanted a white, foaming drink scratched the ground with their fingertips, and milk poured out without limit. Sweet streams of honey meanwhile dripped from their ivy staffs. Had you seen it, you would have prayed to the God you now reject. Then we, your cattlemen and shepherds, gathered to discuss these marvellous, awe-inspiring deeds. One man, who often strayed into town and had a ready tongue, called to us all: "You who live on the terraces of these holy mountains, shall we do our master a favour and chase his mother Agavê out of Bacchus' revels?" We thought that good advice and hid in ambush among the leafy thickets. At the appointed time the women waved their thyrsi for the ceremonies, calling together on Iacchus, King of Clamour, child of Zeus. The mountains and every wild creature were swept into ecstasy; nothing remained unshaken as they rushed on. Agavê happened to leap close to me. I sprang from the thicket where I was hiding and tried to seize her. She shouted, "Ho, my swift-footed hounds, these men are hunting us! Follow me, follow, carrying your thyrsi as spears!" We ran and barely escaped being torn apart by the Bacchanals. Without swords they swooped on our grazing cattle. You would have seen your mother clutching a loudly bellowing heifer with heavy udders, while other women tore calves into bloody strips. Ribs and cloven hoofs flew in every direction; pieces of flesh hung dripping blood beneath the pines. Bulls that had been snorting and glaring fiercely along their horns were tripped and thrown down, dragged to earth by countless clutching hands of girls. The flesh was stripped from their bones faster than you could close your royal eyes. Then they swept on, racing like birds in flight towards the lowland fields along Asopus that yield rich harvests for Thebes: Hysiae and Erythrae, lying beneath Kithairon's cliffs. They descended like an enemy army, throwing possessions everywhere and snatching babies out of houses. Whatever they put on their shoulders stayed there without being tied; nothing fell to the dark ground, neither bronze nor iron. They carried fire on their hair without burning. Furious at being plundered, the inhabitants took up weapons against the Bacchanals. Then, King, we saw something astonishing. The men's iron-pointed javelins drew no blood from them, but the women hurled their thyrsus-staves and inflicted wound after wound. Women drove men into flight, for a God's power was at work. Afterwards they returned to the place they had left, to the springs the God had provided, and washed off the gore. The snakes licked the drops of blood from their cheeks. So, my lord, whoever this God may be, welcome him into the city. Besides his other powers, I hear people say he gave humanity the vine that soothes sorrow. Where wine is absent, Love too disappears, and no other joy remains for human beings.
Chorus. I am afraid to speak freely before the king, but I will still say what I think: Dionysus stands equal to every God.

Pentheus. This Bacchanal outrage is spreading over us like fire, making us a disgrace throughout Greece! There is no time to waste. Go to Electra's gate and summon all my shield-bearing soldiers, the riders of swift horses, those who wield bucklers and those who draw the bow. They are to assemble here with me. We shall march against the Bacchanals. Enduring what these women are doing to us would exceed every limit.

Dionysus. You hear my words, Pentheus, yet you will not give way at all. Even though you insult me, I warn you: remain here and do not take up arms against a God. Bromius will not tolerate your driving his Bacchanals from the mountains where they celebrate.
Pentheus. Don't lecture me. Be satisfied that you escaped your chains, or I shall punish you again.
Dionysus. Better offer him sacrificial victims than rage and kick against the goads, a mortal fighting a God.
Pentheus. Victims? Yes, women, slaughtered as they deserve! Savage killing in the valleys of Kithairon!
Dionysus. You will all run away. What a disgrace when bronze shields retreat before the Bacchanals' wands.
Pentheus. Wrestling with this stranger gets us nowhere. Whether acting or suffering, he refuses to be quiet.
Dionysus. My friend, even now this evil could become something good.
Pentheus. How? By making myself my slave-women's slave?
Dionysus. I can bring the women here without using weapons.
Pentheus. Ha! You are laying a treacherous trap for me here!
Dionysus. A trap? I am trying to save you with my skill!
Pentheus. You have all agreed on this so that your revels can continue forever.
Dionysus. No; understand that I made this agreement with the God.
Pentheus (to attendant). Bring me my weapons! And you, stop talking.
Dionysus. Listen! Would you like to see their camp up in the hills?
Pentheus. Yes, even if the sight cost me an immeasurable fortune in gold.
Dionysus. Why has this longing taken such a powerful hold on you?
Pentheus. To see them drunk on wine—what a bitter spectacle!
Dionysus. Yet a bitter spectacle is something you would enjoy seeing?
Pentheus. Indeed, crouching silently beneath the pine trees to watch them.
Dionysus. However secretly you approach, they will track you down.
Pentheus. Then openly! Yes, that was a useful thing to tell me.
Dionysus. Shall I guide you there? Will you attempt the journey?
Pentheus. Hurry and lead me; I resent every moment of delay!
Dionysus. First you must dress yourself in robes of fine linen.
Pentheus. Why? Am I to stop being a man and become a woman?
Dionysus. Otherwise they may see a man there and kill you.
Pentheus. Good advice. Yes, you have been shrewd about this before.
Dionysus. It was Dionysus who taught me that knowledge.
Pentheus. How do I put this good advice of yours into practice?
Dionysus. I will go inside your palace and dress you there.
Pentheus. Dress me in what? Women's clothes? No, that would shame me.
Dionysus. Have you lost your desire to watch the Maenads now?
Pentheus. Tell me exactly what clothing you intend to put on my body.
Dionysus. I shall adorn your head with long, flowing hair.
Pentheus. And after that, what else will I be wearing?
Dionysus. Long robes, and a coif to cover your head as well.
Pentheus. Is there nothing else you mean to add to my outfit?
Dionysus. A thyrsus to hold, and a spotted fawnskin to wear.
Pentheus. I cannot put a woman's dress around my body!
Dionysus. Then fighting the Maenads will mean bloodshed for you.
Pentheus. Yes, that's true. I must go and observe them first.
Dionysus. Certainly wiser than chasing one disaster into another disaster.
Pentheus. But how can I cross Kadmus' city without being noticed?
Dionysus. We will take deserted paths; I will guide you myself.
Pentheus. Anything would be better than the Bacchants laughing at me.
Dionysus. I will go inside and arrange what is needed.
Pentheus. Very well. My decision is made; I see my course clearly. I am going in. Either I must march out carrying my sword or I must follow the advice you have given. (He leaves.)

Dionysus. Women, he is stepping into the trap. He will find the Bacchants, and death as his punishment. Dionysus, you are close at hand; do your part now and let us take revenge. First strike his mind with a sudden madness. While sane, he would never agree to wear a woman's dress; driven out of his reason, he will put it on. I also long to make him Thebes' laughingstock, led through the city looking like a woman after all his terrifying threats. I am going to put on Pentheus the clothes he will wear to Hades when his mother's hands have killed him. Then he will know Dionysus, Zeus's son, at last revealed as a God most terrible, yet most gentle to humankind. (He leaves.)

chapters.title: Third Stasimon
paragraphs: Chorus. Will my white feet shine in the dancing through another whole night? Will I drift again through the Bacchanal's ecstatic dream, tossing my head into the dew-filled air? Like a fawn playing happily in green pastures after escaping the terror of pursuit, fleeing past the watchers and over their cunningly woven, deadly nets. The huntsmen shout encouragement to the racing dogs, while she bounds desperately across the broad river plain, straining every muscle in bursts of storm-swift speed. At last the trees close their sheltering arms around her, their leafy hair enfolding her in twilight. Happy creature, rescued and hidden from her enemies in the lonely forest where no human follows! What crowning wisdom, what more glorious prize can the Gods grant mortals than to stretch a victorious hand above an enemy's head? Honour, I know, remains precious forever.

Chorus. Heaven's power advances slowly, yet never misses its aim. It teaches a harsh lesson to those who, in their mad imaginings, exalt their disbelief and enthrone it as king: mortals daring to diminish divine things! The Gods wait in a subtle ambush. Time walks onwards, but they never abandon their purpose; merciless fate hunts like a tracking hound until it finds the godless. Neither in our secret thoughts nor in our actions may we put ourselves above the law of established custom. Faith's precious inheritance costs little: trusting the sovereign authority of what heaven sends and of what human nature has sanctioned through age after age. What crowning wisdom, what more glorious prize can the Gods grant mortals than to stretch a victorious hand above an enemy's head? Honour, I know, remains precious forever.

Chorus. Blessed is the one who escapes the ravenous sea and reaches a peaceful harbour; blessed the one who succeeds after labour and struggle. One person rises higher in wealth or power than another, yet countless hopes still burn in countless hearts. Some ripen into fulfilment; others end in nothing. Happy the person whose joy increases with each passing day. (Dionysus enters.)

chapters.title: Fourth Episode
paragraphs: Dionysus. Pentheus, burning to see forbidden things, so eager in your wrongful eagerness, come outside your palace. Let me see you dressed as a woman, in a frenzied Bacchant's clothes, ready to spy on your mother and her company. (Pentheus enters.) There: you have the appearance of one of Kadmus' daughters.

Pentheus. Ah! I seem to be looking at two suns, two versions of Thebes, our city with seven gates! You look like a bull leading me onwards, and horns have grown upon your head. Were you an animal before? You are certainly a bull now!
Dionysus. The God is accompanying us. He was unfriendly before, but now he is our ally; you see as you should at last.
Pentheus. Who do I look like? Don't I have Ino's bearing, or the way my mother Agavê carries herself?
Dionysus. When I look at you, I seem to see the women themselves. But what's this? A lock has slipped out of position, away from where I braided it beneath your coif.
Pentheus. I disarranged it inside, shaking my head backwards and forwards as I whirled in Bacchic frenzy.
Dionysus. Since I have taken on the work of your lady's maid, I will put it right. Lift your head.
Pentheus. There you are; smooth it into place. I am relying on you.
Dionysus. Your belt is loose now, and the folds of your dress do not hang evenly below your ankles.
Pentheus. Yes, it looks wrong beside my right foot. On the left the robe hangs straight along the tendon.
Dionysus. When you find the Bacchants sober and your expectations disappointed, you will surely call me your best friend.
Pentheus. Should I carry this thyrsus in this hand or the other, to look more like a proper Bacchanal?
Dionysus. Carry it on the right, moving it in time with your right foot. How admirable your change of heart is!
Pentheus. Could I lift the valleys of Mount Kithairon onto my shoulders, with all the Bacchanals as well?
Dionysus. You could, if you wished. Before, your mind was crooked; now it has the shape it should have.
Pentheus. Using levers? Or could I tear it up with my hands, pushing an arm or shoulder beneath its peaks?
Dionysus. No, don't destroy the Nymphs' shrines or the places where Pan lives and the sound of his pipes echoes.
Pentheus. True, true. We must not overpower the women by force. I shall hide among the pine trees.
Dionysus. You will have the hiding place fate appoints, coming as you do in deceit to spy upon the Bacchanals.
Pentheus. I think I can see them in the thickets, caught like birds in the snares of their sweet love-play.
Dionysus. That is precisely what you are appointed to watch for. Perhaps you will catch them, unless they catch you first.
Pentheus. Take me straight through the centre of Thebes. I alone among them dare to undertake this deed.
Dionysus. You alone are labouring for Thebes, entirely alone. That is why your appointed strain and struggle await you. Follow me; I will guide you there in safety. Someone else will bring you back.
Pentheus. Yes, my own mother will.
Dionysus. Everyone will see you then.
Pentheus. That is why I am going.
Dionysus. You will return carried high.
Pentheus. What luxurious comfort for me!
Dionysus. Your mother's hands will carry you.
Pentheus. You mean to lavish splendour on me!
Dionysus. Only the appropriate splendour for you.
Pentheus. The splendour that I deserve.

Dionysus. Strange man, strange indeed! What happens to you will be strange too. In this way you will gain fame reaching to the heavens. (Pentheus leaves.) Agavê, reach out your hands; you sisters, daughters of Kadmus, reach out yours! I am bringing this prince to a mighty contest. The victory will belong to me and to Bromius. Its outcome will reveal the rest. (He leaves.)

chapters.title: Fourth Stasimon
paragraphs: Chorus. Rise, swift hell-hounds of Madness! Race into the mountain valleys where Kadmus' daughters celebrate. Sting them into fury so they tear apart the man who has come dressed as a woman to spy on the Bacchanals, the madness-stricken fool! His mother will see him first, watching their actions from a rock worn by water or a tree split by storms. Her cry will ring down to the Maenads: "Who has come here along the mountain paths to spy on Kadmus' daughters, the girls who race across the hills, our Bacchanal sisters? What mother gave birth to such a creature? Who was she, who? I think no woman's blood produced him. He must have sprung from a lioness, the forest's scourge, or perhaps from those demons, the Gorgons of Libya." Justice, approach us, come close with your avenging sword. Kill this unrighteous offspring of earth-born Echion. Cut clean through his throat: he fears neither God nor law.

Chorus. See how he comes, impious and lawless, driven mad by spite, to fight your rites and your mother's, Bacchus, trying with his powerless strength to overthrow what cannot be conquered! A person can win a life without sorrow by keeping the spirit sober and obeying heaven promptly, without complaint or attempts to reach beyond a mortal's limits. I desire no such presumptuous cleverness. I seek instead—and the search itself makes me happy—the things it cannot know: the great, glorious wisdom revealed from everlasting days. I would shape my life in purity and holiness, pursue noble aims from dawn until the day's death, honour the Gods and refuse the road of injustice. Justice, approach us, come close with your avenging sword. Kill this unrighteous offspring of earth-born Echion. Cut clean through his throat: he fears neither God nor law.

Chorus. Dionysus, show yourself! Appear as a bull, or take the form of a dragon, a many-headed monster, or a lion whose limbs are wrapped in dazzling flame. Come, Bacchus, and smile in mockery as you surround him with destruction's net. Let the hunter be bound among the crowded Maenads, caught by the quarry he set out to find. (A Messenger enters.)
